summary: A seal legend that closes with sign 820 marks its holder as belonging to an upper grade, and seals for that grade were cut larger. We measure size as residual log face area: the logarithm of the face area minus the value expected for a seal of the same type, site class (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Lothal, Chanhu-daro, Kalibangan or other) and length. Across both halves of the corpus the ten seals ending in 820 average about +0.64 on this scale, nearly twice the face area of comparable seals, and six of the ten are among the 25 largest residuals of their half. On the photographs, 820 stands at full height and normal spacing at the closing end of the legend, as any closing sign does. This is the surviving form of the claim frozen for Shot A, the single frozen test of this card. The frozen version named four closing signs (001, 595, 679, 820). Its central prediction passed on the confirmation half, but the adversarial review found the pass carried by three seals ending in 820, and 679 did not repeat its discovery-half effect. We formed the narrowed claim after seeing the outcome, and it has had no test of its own.
title: A legend closing in sign 820 marks an upper grade, cut on a larger seal

summary: Indus legends are built from seven word classes: numerals, links, the names of great households, personal-name elements, commodities and units, office nouns, and closing determinatives, signs that classify the word before them. A seal legend reads "of [household]: [personal name], [department] [office] [the man or the body]". The pair of short strokes after the opening signs 817, 861 and 820 is a particle meaning "of"; the fish signs are "star" elements of personal names; the jar 740 is the steward of the store named by the sign before it; the comb 400 marks an office as a body, and the man 090 an individual holder. Harappa's moulded and incised tablets are tokens of standard measures, offices and labour; Mohenjo-daro's copper tablets record named holders and their fodder or grain allotments; pottery marks give capacities in standard units or the store a vessel belongs to. Names and commodities belong to a city, while households, offices and grammar are shared, and office holders have larger seals bearing the emblem of the shared administration. The classes therefore predict where seals were found, their size, their animal and their date. The full map is GLOSS-MAP.json and the reading READING.md.
title: A working reading of Indus legends as household, name and office

summary: The animal on an Indus seal marks the holder's affiliation, and the unicorn affiliation was a single body present in every city. Rarer animals mark smaller affiliations, each based in fewer places. The affiliation is shown by the animal and is not written in the legend, so holders of the same title in different affiliations carry the same text with different animals.
title: The unicorn marks one affiliation present in every city

summary: The four-sign text carried by the Lothal sealings L-161 to L-170, clay impressions of a seal, and by the Mohenjo-daro seal fragment M-895 is the title of an office, held by different people in the two cities. The Lothal sealings were made with a different seal from M-895, cut for a holder of the same office in another affiliation, which is why the sealings show an elephant and M-895 a unicorn.
title: The text shared by Lothal L-161 and Mohenjo-daro M-895 names an office

summary: Harappa's moulded and incised tablets are standard tokens issued in series. One face names what the token is for, and the face with two, three or four tall strokes before sign 700 states its tier: two, three or four of a standard unit. On seals, by contrast, stroke groups are fixed parts of names and titles and do not count goods.
title: Tall strokes before sign 700 count tiers on Harappa tokens

summary: At Mohenjo-daro the stock of signs that close seal legends was fixed before the lowest levels the excavators reached, and it did not change while the city was rebuilt above them. Sign 740 and eleven other closing signs (520, 090, 400, 151, 156, 527, 617, 621, 226, 892 and 407) close about three legends in four at every height of an excavated sequence, and the two-sign closing formulae, most of them ending in 740, close about one legend in three at every height. The front of the legend was not fixed. The choice of opening sign, the variant cut within a sign class and the length of the legend drifted through the sequence, so that seals from the top of an area's deposits open with different signs, use different variants and run longer than seals from its bottom.
title: The closing stock of Mohenjo-daro seal legends was fixed from the lowest levels

summary: Fish combinations form an ordered designation field within seal legends. Successive fish forms carry different parts of one compound label. The field can identify a person, affiliation, office or category; its component sounds remain unassigned.
title: Fish combinations form an ordered designation field

summary: Short-stroke groups immediately before plain fish on seals chiefly form the asterism names three-star, six-star and seven-star. Their distribution follows a fixed celestial-name inventory.
title: Three, six and seven asterism names cover short-stroke fish combinations on seals

summary: H-912 B records four vessel-units of fish. The stroke group gives the number, the V-shaped sign names the vessel unit, and the fish-shaped sign names the contents.
title: H-912 B records four vessel-units of fish

summary: The Indus seal legend was written to one fixed pattern through the urban period, and the seal that carried it changed around it. At Harappa, from the end of Period 3B to the end of Period 3C, some three to four centuries of Vats's Mound F sequence, the same fifteen signs close about seven legends in ten (740 above all, then 520, 405, 154, 090 and the rest of the stock shared with Mohenjo-daro), the same signs open them, the same variants are cut within each sign class, legends keep their length, and no sign enters or leaves the inventory with the period. When the long rectangular seal with script alone arrives in Period 3C it takes the same legend. Mohenjo-daro's legends show the same pattern at the bottom and top of both excavated sequences. The legend was a standard already in place before the earliest seals these excavations reached, and each city kept it while it rebuilt.
title: The seal legend kept one fixed pattern through Harappa's Periods 3B and 3C

summary: Proto-Dravidian mīn meant both "fish" and "star". The ancestor of all Dravidian languages, spoken about 4,400 years ago, called a star "the shining one" with a word built on miṉ "to shine", and that word had the same form as mīn "fish", so a writer of the third millennium BCE could draw a fish to write "star". Parpola's astral reading of the Indus fish sign rests on this pun.
title: Proto-Dravidian mīn meant both fish and star

summary: The short-stroke, plain-V and plain-fish Harappa tablet series specifies a standard four-unit record indexed to the Fish category. V supplies the unit role; fish supplies a category role that is also expressed in the longer legend on the other face. The category can identify contents, an account or a recipient. Four is this construction's denomination.
title: The plain-fish tablet series records a standard four-unit category

summary: A run of fish signs in the name part of an Indus seal legend is the holder's birth-star name, the name of the asterism the moon occupied at his or her birth. The runs form a closed class of about 30 to 40 names, built from five common fish forms (in the project's sign coding: plain, top-marked, capped, barred and inner-marked) and their ordered combinations, and the plain fish is the favourite, as Puṣya is in the early Brāhmī donor lists. The stroke groups written before a fish are a separate element of the legend and not part of the star name.
title: Fish runs on seals are birth-star names

summary: The interlocking Dravidian readings that Asko Parpola presents for the Indus script record the density of the Old Tamil compound vocabulary and the choice of the sign sequences he examined, not the language of the inscriptions. Applied to sign sequences chosen before any Tamil compound is looked up, his procedure finds attested interlocks for his word assignments no more often than for random Tamil words of the same compounding productivity and frequency.
title: Parpola's interlocks measure the Tamil lexicon, not the script

summary: Harappan builders aligned the main axes of each new town on the setting point of a bright star or star group on the western horizon, so that a town's deviation from the cardinal directions records the year it was laid out. In the Pleiades version every town is turned clockwise, by about half a degree more for each century of later layout; in the Aldebaran version towns laid out before about 2050 BCE are turned anticlockwise and later towns clockwise.
title: Harappan towns were laid out on the setting point of a star

summary: The builders of the Indus-plain cities fixed true north by observing the sky and laid out Harappa's Mound F, the house blocks of Mohenjo-daro and the Lothal dock within two degrees of it. The walled towns of Kutch, Saurashtra and the Ghaggar plain were set out on local axes that follow the landform beside them, the river channel, ridge or shoreline, and are turned anticlockwise from the cardinal directions by 5 to 30 degrees. A town's deviation records its setting, not its date.
title: The plains cities were laid out on true north, the regional towns on their landform

summary: Indus building groups changed their houses under common rules that preserved shared routes and services. The repeated unit of urban coordination was the connection between adjacent groups through streets, drains and entrances. Districts could grow, subdivide or change orientation while those rules continued. Local negotiation was one means of maintaining them.
title: Shared urban routes survived rebuilding through common rules

summary: Indus sealings recorded responsibility at handovers between urban groups. Their recurring legends connected institutions across districts and towns, while the particular stamp identified an authorising holder. The relevant architectural settings were controlled passages, storage access and points where goods changed custody.
title: Sealings recorded handovers between urban groups

summary: Harappa's repeated tablet series recorded obligations or entitlements for work on shared infrastructure. The repeated descriptor identified a work group or service and the varying stroke group identified an obligation class. Production batches made comparable records available to several participants.
title: Harappa tablet series recorded obligations for shared work

summary: Farming households and local specialist networks carried practical knowledge across the decline of Indus urban institutions. Operations that could be maintained through local materials, recurring work and teaching survived more readily than operations dependent on distant procurement or large coordinating networks.
title: Local farming and craft networks carried practical knowledge beyond Indus cities

summary: Early Indo-Aryan-speaking communities acquired some regional crop knowledge and agricultural vocabulary through contact with farming communities carrying older South Asian practices. This contact contributed to the agricultural world described in Vedic texts. The transmitted knowledge crossed language boundaries.
title: Language contact carried regional farming knowledge into early Indo-Aryan communities

summary: A diagnostic operation preserved within a Vedic farming rite descends through regional farming communities from an Indus-period practice. Later specialists placed that inherited operation within a changed ritual and explanatory system.
title: A Vedic farming rite preserves a regional operation transmitted from the Indus period
